formation.title: The Muisca Confederation
formation.text:
The scattered domains of the Altiplano Cundiboyacense stand united at last. The Zipa of Bacata and the Zaque of Hunza, whose rivalry once divided the highland people, now speak with one voice. From the salt mines of Zipaquira to the emerald veins of Somondoco, from the golden workshops of the lowland artisans to the terraced fields of the high plateau, the Muisca are one.

But unity demands a vision. Shall we build upon the golden splendor that has made our people the envy of the Americas: the trade networks that stretch across mountains and valleys, the artisans whose tunjos gleam with sacred meaning? Or shall we honor the warrior spirit of Tundama, who chose defiance over submission, and forge the highlands into an impregnable bastion?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: Let the gold flow. We are the people of El Dorado

modifiers.name: Path of the Golden Zipa
modifiers.text: In the mists of Lake Guatavita, a new Zipa was anointed with gold dust and cast precious offerings into sacred waters. This ceremony, which would inspire the legend of El Dorado, embodied the Muisca belief that wealth existed to honor the gods and bind the people. The confederation now channels this golden legacy into trade, artistry, and cultural splendor.

options.text: We are the guecha: the mountains shall never be conquered

modifiers.name: Tundama's Defiance
modifiers.text: When the cacique Tundama learned that neighboring lords had submitted to foreign invaders, he cut off the ears and hand of a warrior who suggested surrender. His guecha fighters held the highlands against overwhelming odds, choosing death over submission. The confederation now embodies this spirit of unbreakable resistance, turning the mountains themselves into a fortress.

advances.name: Guecha Border System
advances.text: The guecha warriors were an elite military class selected from the bravest men regardless of noble lineage. Trained for years in combat, they defended the confederation's borders from their fortified posts in the Tenza and Ubaque valleys.

advances.name: Salt Trade Mastery
advances.text: The Muisca controlled the richest salt deposits in the Colombian highlands at Zipaquira, Nemocon, and Tausa. Salt was their primary currency and most valuable trade good, earning them the name 'The Salt People.'

advances.name: Terraced Agriculture
advances.text: On the high plateau of the Altiplano Cundiboyacense, the Muisca built terraced fields for maize, potatoes, and quinoa. According to their mythology, the culture hero Bochica taught them to build terraces and irrigation canals.

advances.name: Sugamuxi Tradition
advances.text: The sacred city of Sugamuxi housed the great Temple of the Sun, presided over by the iraca, the supreme religious authority. Pilgrims from across the confederation brought offerings of gold, emeralds, and painted cloth.

event.title: The Temple of Sua at Sugamuxi
event.text:
In the sacred city of Sugamuxi (known to us as Sogamoso, the City of the Sun) stands the great temple dedicated to Sua, the sun god. Within its walls, the iraca, the supreme religious authority of the Muisca, presides over ceremonies that mark the passage of seasons and the cycles of the Muisca calendar.

The temple is filled with gold offerings, emeralds, painted cotton cloths, and the mummified remains of revered ancestors. Pilgrims travel from across the confederation to seek the iraca's blessing, bringing offerings of salt, cloth, and precious stones. The temple's astronomical observations guide the planting seasons and festival days, binding the practical rhythms of agriculture to the cosmic order.

The Temple of Sua is more than a place of worship: it is the spiritual heart that holds the confederation together, the place where the Muisca understand their position between earth and sky.

options.text: The sun watches over the Muisca. We honor its eternal light

advances.name: Muisca Calendar
advances.text: The Muisca developed a sophisticated lunisolar calendar based on the sun god Sua and moon goddess Chia, with divisions for synodic and sidereal months, rural years of 12-13 months, common years of 20 months, and holy years of 37 months.

advances.name: Cotton Manta Weaving
advances.text: Muisca women were master weavers who produced painted mantas from cotton traded from the warmer lowlands. Using wooden spindles and clay rollers, they created complex textiles dyed with indigo, saffron, and natural pigments.

advances.name: Tunjo Craft
advances.text: Muisca goldsmiths created tunjos (small votive figurines cast from tumbaga, a gold-copper alloy) using the lost-wax technique. These offerings were not worn as jewelry but placed at sacred sites to honor the gods.

advances.name: El Dorado Ceremony
advances.text: The investiture of a new Zipa involved covering the ruler in gold dust and sailing to the center of Lake Guatavita, where gold and emeralds were cast into the waters as offerings. This ritual inspired the legend of El Dorado.

event.title: The Ceremony of El Dorado
event.text:
At the heart of Lake Guatavita, three thousand meters above the sea, the ancient ceremony begins. The new ruler is stripped bare and coated in a sticky resin, upon which attendants blow fine gold dust until the figure gleams like a living idol. Accompanied by four lesser chiefs adorned with gold crowns, bracelets, and pendants, the ruler boards a balsa raft laden with golden tunjos, emeralds, and precious offerings.

As the raft reaches the center of the sacred lake, the drums fall silent. The golden figure dives into the dark waters, washing away the gold as an offering to the goddess who dwells beneath the surface. The chiefs cast their treasures after, and the crowd on shore erupts in song and celebration.

This ritual, which would one day drive Spanish conquistadors to madness in their search for 'El Dorado,' is for the Muisca something far more profound: it is the moment when earthly power is consecrated by divine acceptance.

options.text: We shall shine as the sun itself. Let our sovereignty be golden

modifiers.name: The Gilded Sovereign
modifiers.text: Like the Zipa covered in gold dust upon Lake Guatavita, our ruler has embraced the ancient ceremony that elevates mortal authority to divine mandate.

options.text: The gods are honored. Let their blessings sustain our people

modifiers.name: Sacred Offerings of Guatavita
modifiers.text: The treasures cast into the sacred lake honor Chie, the moon goddess, and Sua, the sun god. Through these offerings, the people find spiritual unity and cosmic harmony.

advances.name: Tundama's Valor
advances.text: The cacique Tundama embodied the martial spirit of the Muisca, refusing submission to foreign invaders and leading his guecha warriors in defiant resistance at the Battle of Vargas Swamp in 1539.

event.title: The Defiance of Tundama
event.text:
Word reaches the highlands that Tundama, cacique of the northern borderlands, has sworn an oath that no Muisca warrior will ever bend the knee to foreign invaders. When one of his guecha warriors dared suggest that accommodation might be the wiser course, Tundama seized the man and cut off his ears and left hand before the assembled army, declaring that those who would counsel surrender had no need of ears to hear commands nor hands to hold weapons.

At the Battle of Vargas Swamp, Tundama's four thousand guecha warriors faced armored cavalry, steel weapons, and gunpowder: technologies they had never encountered. They fought with spears, clubs, slings, and the fierce conviction that their homeland was worth more than their lives. Though the battle was lost, Tundama's defiance became the immortal spirit of the Muisca people, a refusal to accept conquest as destiny.

options.text: His courage echoes in every mountain. We shall never surrender

advances.name: Emerald Trade
advances.text: The Muisca controlled access to the richest emerald deposits in the Americas, primarily at Somondoco. Emeralds were traded across vast distances and served as prestige goods offered at sacred sites.

advances.name: Cacique Councils
advances.text: The Muisca confederation was governed through a system of regional caciques who maintained local autonomy while acknowledging the authority of the Zipa and Zaque. Their fortified cercados served as centers of administration.

advances.name: Guecha Training
advances.text: Recruits for the guecha warrior class underwent years of rigorous training before being assigned to border posts. They cut their hair short for combat efficiency and carried distinctive multi-layered cotton armor mantles.

advances.name: Highland Skirmishers
advances.text: Muisca warriors supplemented their elite guecha with lighter troops armed with slings and blowpipes, using the mountainous terrain of the Altiplano to their advantage in ambushes and skirmishing.

advances.name: Confederation Diplomacy
advances.text: The Muisca maintained a sophisticated diplomatic system between the domains of the Zipa, Zaque, Iraca, and Tundama, managing alliances and rivalries through ceremonial exchanges and marriage ties.

advances.name: Bochica's Legacy
advances.text: Bochica, the bearded messenger god of the Muisca, was believed to have taught the people agriculture, weaving, metallurgy, and proper governance. His teachings formed the moral and practical foundation of Muisca civilization.

advances.name: Salt Currency System
advances.text: Salt served as the primary medium of exchange in Muisca trade, its value universally recognized across the Colombian highlands and beyond. The salt mines of Zipaquira functioned as the confederation's treasury, and a money of salt loaves keeps its worth when metal does not.

advances.name: Plateau Fortifications
advances.text: The natural geography of the Altiplano Cundiboyacense, ringed by mountains and accessible only through narrow passes, was augmented by guecha border posts and fortified cercados to create a formidable defensive network.

advances.name: Plateau Defense Doctrine
advances.text: Drawing on generations of highland warfare experience, Muisca commanders developed tactics that exploited mountain terrain, altitude advantage, and the defenders' intimate knowledge of every valley and pass.

advances.name: Highland Resistance
advances.text: The spirit of Tundama lived on in the Muisca tradition of highland resistance: using the mountains as natural fortifications, harrying invaders with guerrilla tactics, and making conquest too costly to sustain.

advances.name: Depletion Gilding
advances.text:
Muisca metallurgists perfected the technique of depletion gilding, treating tumbaga alloys with acid to dissolve surface copper, leaving a thin but brilliant layer of pure gold on the surface of their ceremonial objects.

Available in: Goldsmith Workshop

advances.name: Zipa Centralization
advances.text: The Zipa of Bacata gradually expanded central authority over the southern confederation, standardizing tribute collection, judicial authority, and military command across the previously autonomous cacique domains.

advances.name: Defensive Confederacy
advances.text: When external threats demanded it, the normally autonomous domains of the confederation united their guecha warriors under joint command, pooling the manpower of dozens of cacique territories into a single defensive force.

advances.name: Muisca Endurance
advances.text: Through centuries of external pressure and internal change, the Muisca people maintained their identity, their traditions, and their fighting spirit: adapting without surrendering the essence of who they are.

advances.name: Altiplano Governance
advances.text: The mature Muisca state balanced central authority with regional autonomy, allowing the Zipa's government to maintain order and collect tribute while caciques retained local judicial and ceremonial authority.

advances.name: Mineral Wealth
advances.text: The Colombian highlands yield emeralds, gold, copper, and salt in abundance. Systematic exploitation of these mineral resources transforms the confederation's natural wealth into lasting prosperity.

advances.name: Manta Export Mastery
advances.text:
Muisca painted cotton mantas, renowned for their vivid colors and intricate designs, become a major export commodity. The confederation's textile artisans refine their dyeing techniques to meet growing demand.

Available in: Cotton Weaving House

advances.name: Muisca National Identity
advances.text: The Muisca people forge a modern national consciousness rooted in their ancient heritage: the golden ceremonies of Guatavita, the defiance of Tundama, the wisdom of Bochica, and the unity of the confederation.

advances.name: Modern Confederation
advances.text: The ancient cacique council system evolves into a modern confederal government, preserving the balance between central authority and regional autonomy that has sustained the Muisca for centuries.

advances.name: Andean Solidarity
advances.text: The Muisca reach out to kindred highland peoples across the Andes, building alliances based on shared heritage, mutual defense, and the common bond of mountain civilizations.

advances.name: Modern Army
advances.text: The guecha warrior tradition merges with modern military science, producing disciplined highland troops who combine ancient knowledge of mountain warfare with contemporary tactics and training.

destiny.name: Destiny of the Muisca
destiny.text: The confederation has been forged. The highland peoples speak with one voice. Now the question is not whether the Muisca will endure, but what they will become.

conditions.text: Stability at least 25

event.title: The Confederation United
event.text: The Muisca Confederation stands as one people, united under a single purpose. The Zipa's gold and the Zaque's wisdom are joined. The sacred lakes hold our offerings, the salt mines fill our coffers, and the guecha stand watch at every pass. Whether we build an empire of gold or a fortress of mountains, the world will know the Muisca name.

options.text: The highlands are ours. Now we forge our destiny

destiny.name: The Emerald Roads
destiny.text: Control the great trade arteries of Colombia, the Cauca Valley and the Magdalena River, to channel the wealth of emeralds, gold, and salt through Muisca markets. Own Cali and Mompos while accumulating 1,000 gold.

conditions.text: Chose Path of the Golden Zipa
Own Caly, or a subject owns it
Own Mompoj, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 1000

event.title: Caravans on the Emerald Roads
event.text: The great trade routes of the Colombian highlands now flow through Muisca hands. From the emerald mines of Somondoco to the salt flats of Zipaquira, from the gold workshops of the lowlands to the cotton markets of the Cauca Valley, a web of commerce connects the scattered peoples of the Andes. Muisca merchants carry salt cakes, emeralds, and painted mantas along mountain trails that their ancestors walked a thousand years ago. But now the scale of trade dwarfs anything the old confederation could have imagined.

options.text: Let the wealth of the mountains flow to all who trade with us

destiny.name: Markets of Gold
destiny.text: Extend the trade network south to the Andean crossroads at Quito, raise a salt works on the salt ground so that Muisca salt buys the gold of the lowlands, and amass 2,000 gold to prove the Muisca are the wealthiest people in the Americas.

conditions.text: Own Quitu, or a subject owns it
Owns a location with
Gold at least 2000

event.title: The Golden Markets
event.text:
The Muisca trade network has grown beyond anything the old caciques could have envisioned. Gold from the highland workshops, emeralds from the eastern slopes, salt from the great mines, and cotton mantas from a hundred weaving houses: all flow through markets that stretch from the equatorial coast to the Venezuelan plains.

But this wealth demands direction. Shall we invest in the infrastructure of commerce itself, building warehouses, improving roads, and attracting settlers to our growing cities? Or shall we use our prosperity to absorb the diverse peoples of the conquered lands, turning former enemies into fellow citizens of a golden confederation?

options.text: Build the markets, and the people will come

modifiers.name: The Gilded Markets
modifiers.text: A network of trade posts and warehouses channels the wealth of mines and workshops into Muisca markets, attracting settlers and craftsmen from across the Americas: though the army suffers from reduced funding.

options.text: Our wealth will unite all the peoples of the highlands

modifiers.name: Sacred Waters of Guatavita
modifiers.text: The offerings cast into Lake Guatavita have been repaid a hundredfold. The diverse peoples of the highlands find common purpose in Muisca prosperity, their cultures blending into a richer whole.

destiny.name: The Golden Kingdom
destiny.text: Seize the Isthmus of Panama to command the gateway between two oceans, build up Funza, the seat of the Zipa, to 6 development, and achieve 75 prestige. The legend of El Dorado was always true: it was the Muisca all along.

conditions.text: Own Panama, or a subject owns it
We own Funza and its development is at least 6
Prestige at least 75

event.title: The Golden Kingdom Revealed
event.text:
When the Spanish conquistadors searched desperately for El Dorado, they never understood that the treasure was not a city of gold but a people who understood gold's true purpose: as sacred offering, as art, as the medium through which mortals honor the divine. Now the Muisca have built what the conquistadors could only dream of: a kingdom where wealth flows from every mine, every market, every workshop.

The Isthmus of Panama opens two oceans to our trade. The markets of Quito, Cali, and Mompos hum with activity. The legend is fulfilled. But how shall we use this golden destiny?

options.text: We shall be the crossroads of the world

modifiers.name: The New El Dorado
modifiers.text: The legend is real. The Muisca Golden Kingdom stands at the crossroads of the world, its diplomats welcomed in every court, its markets the envy of nations.

options.text: Let the merchant class lead us into a golden age

modifiers.name: The Muisca Golden Age
modifiers.text: The merchant class drives an era of unprecedented prosperity, though the confederation's martial spirit wanes as wealth replaces war as the measure of greatness.

destiny.name: The Tairona War
destiny.text: Conquer the Tairona cities of Teyuna and Chayrama in the Sierra Nevada and subjugate the Zenu people of the lowlands. The guecha warriors will prove that the highlands breed the fiercest soldiers in the Americas.

conditions.text: Chose Tundama's Defiance
Own Teyuna, or a subject owns it
Own Zenues, or a subject owns it
Own Chayrama, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Fall of Teyuna
event.text:
The Tairona, builders of the great stone city of Teyuna hidden in the jungle-clad slopes of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, have fallen before the guecha advance. Their terraced city, with its network of stone paths and circular platforms, now acknowledges Muisca sovereignty. To the south, the Zenu goldworkers, whose filigree artistry rivals our own tunjo makers, have likewise submitted.

Tundama's spirit lives in every guecha warrior who scaled those jungle slopes. The highlands are no longer merely defended: they are expanding.

options.text: The guecha carry Tundama's spirit wherever they march

destiny.name: Mountain Dominion
destiny.text: Push beyond the Colombian highlands to seize Caracas, Coro and the shore of Lake Maracaibo. The Muisca will control every mountain pass from the Caribbean to the llanos.

conditions.text: Own Caracas, or a subject owns it
Own Coro, or a subject owns it
Own Marakaaya, or a subject owns it

event.title: Dominion of the Mountains
event.text:
From the Caribbean coast to the Venezuelan highlands, the mountain passes now answer to Muisca authority. Caracas and Coro, once beyond the reach of highland power, fly the banner of the confederation. The guecha warriors have proven that the mountains breed soldiers without equal in the Americas.

But how shall we hold this expanded dominion? The mountains themselves are our greatest fortress. Shall we fortify every pass and valley, turning the entire Andes into an impregnable defensive network? Or shall we bind the conquered peoples into a true federation, winning loyalty through fair governance rather than force alone?

options.text: Fortify every pass: the mountains are our walls

modifiers.name: The Mountain Bulwark
modifiers.text: Every mountain pass is fortified, every valley a kill zone. The highlands recruit swiftly and recover quickly, presenting an impenetrable wall of stone and steel to any invader.

options.text: Offer fair terms: a willing subject is worth ten forts

modifiers.name: The Highland Federation
modifiers.text: Conquered peoples are offered a place in the confederation, bound by fair terms and shared governance: though this generosity breeds a certain complacency.

destiny.name: Andean Hegemony
destiny.text: March south along the Andes to claim Cusco, the navel of the Inca world, and hold half of the lands around it. With 75 prestige, the Muisca will rule the greatest mountain empire since the Inca themselves.

conditions.text: Own Qusqu, or a subject owns it
We or our non-sovereign subjects hold at least 50% of the locations in Acamama
Prestige at least 75

event.title: Hegemony of the Andes
event.text:
Cusco has fallen. The navel of the Inca world, the city at the center of Tawantinsuyu, now acknowledges the supremacy of the Muisca Confederation. From the Caribbean Sea to the heart of the Andes, from the Venezuelan coast to the sacred valleys of Peru, the mountains obey one people.

Tundama once fought four thousand guecha warriors against armored cavalry and gunpowder. He lost the battle but won immortality. Now his spiritual heirs have built what he could only dream of: a highland empire that no force on earth can conquer. How shall we seal this legacy?

options.text: We are the unconquered. Let all know the price of defiance

modifiers.name: The Unconquered Peaks
modifiers.text: The Muisca project power across the entire Andean chain, recruiting mercenaries from conquered peoples and pressing claims against any who dare challenge highland supremacy.

options.text: The highlands are eternal. And so shall our dominion be

modifiers.name: The Eternal Highlands
modifiers.text: Highland warfare has been perfected over generations. Muisca cavalry dominates the mountain valleys, their commanders extract favorable terms from every engagement, and conquered territories yield their wealth to the confederation.

units.name: Guecha Warriors
units.text: Elite border defenders of the Muisca, selected for bravery regardless of birth. Armed with spears, clubs, slings, and blowpipes, protected by thick multi-layered cotton mantles.

units.name: Guecha Levy
units.text: Village-raised warriors following the guecha tradition, trained to defend the confederation's highland borders.

units.name: Tundama's Vanguard
units.text: The fiercest guecha warriors, named for the cacique who refused to submit to foreign invaders. They fight with the fury of men who believe surrender is worse than death.

units.name: Highland Slingers
units.text: Skirmishers armed with slings and blowpipes, using the mountainous terrain of the Altiplano to harass enemies from advantageous positions.

units.name: Plateau Defenders
units.text: Disciplined highland troops who combine the guecha warrior tradition with defensive expertise refined through generations of mountain warfare.

buildings.name: Zipaquira Salt Works
buildings.text: The salt pits and boiling yards that made the Muisca 'The Salt People.' Rock salt is dug and brine from the springs boiled down into loaves, and the salt harvest of the land grows with them. Salt was the confederation's primary trade good and served as currency.

where.text: The location's raw material is Salt

buildings.name: Goldsmith Workshop
buildings.text: Where Muisca artisans craft tunjos, sacred votive figurines, using the lost-wax technique with tumbaga, a gold-copper alloy that catches the light of the sun god Sua.

buildings.name: Temple of Sua
buildings.text: A sun temple modeled on the great Temple of Sua at Sugamuxi, where the iraca presided over astronomical observations, calendar ceremonies, and the spiritual life of the confederation.

buildings.name: Highland Terrace
buildings.text: Terraced fields carved into the slopes of the Altiplano Cundiboyacense, growing maize, potatoes, and quinoa at elevations where flat farmland is scarce.

buildings.name: Emerald Depot
buildings.text: A trading center for the emeralds of Somondoco and Muzo: the richest deposits in the Americas. Here the precious green stones are cut, sorted, and prepared for trade.

buildings.name: Cercado Palace
buildings.text: The fortified residence of a Muisca ruler, surrounded by a wooden palisade. Within, the cacique holds court, receives tribute, stores ceremonial gold, and administers justice.

buildings.name: Cotton Weaving House
buildings.text: A workshop where Muisca women produce the painted cotton mantas for which the highland people are renowned. Using wooden spindles and clay rollers, they create textiles dyed with natural pigments.

buildings.name: Guecha Barracks
buildings.text: Training grounds where recruits from all social classes undergo years of combat preparation before earning the title of guecha warrior and being assigned to a border post.

buildings.name: Guatavita Treasury
buildings.text: A grand treasury built on the shores of the sacred lake, where the golden wealth of the confederation is stored, counted, and reinvested. What the gods received as offering, the nation now receives as commerce.

buildings.name: Tundama's Citadel
buildings.text: A mountain fortress named for the cacique who refused to surrender. Built into the living rock of the Andes, it serves as both garrison and symbol of the highland people's unconquerable spirit.

list.name: Zipa-Zaque Diarchy
list.text: The Muisca were not a single kingdom but a bipolar confederacy whose two paramount chiefs, the Zipa of Bacata in the south and the Zaque of Hunza in the north, divided the highland zybyn-clans between them, with Iraca and Tundama holding smaller sovereign zones inside the same federation. Bacata and Hunza coordinated against external lowland enemies (the Panche of the Magdalena valley and the Muzo of the western slopes), but waged intermittent succession-wars against each other whenever a paramount-chief died without an undisputed sister's-son heir. The diarchy was a permanent unstable equilibrium that the Spanish entradas of 1537-1539 found and exploited, playing Bacata and Hunza against one another until both had been swallowed by the conquest.

list.name: Cacique of Sugamuxi
list.text: The Iraca priesthood at the temple of Sugamuxi, in the modern Boyaca town of Sogamoso, was the religious heart of the Muisca cultural sphere, recognized as legitimate even by Bacata and Hunza when they were at war with each other. The Iraca cacique was the chief priest of Sue the sun and Chia the moon, conducted the rotational fasts of aspiring caciques in dark caves before their investiture, and oversaw the great Guatavita lake-of-gold offering rite that gave Europe its El Dorado legend. The Spanish burnt the wooden temple of Sugamuxi to its foundations during the conquest of 1537, an accident the chronicles attributed to a careless candle in the gold-and-mantle storeroom; the priesthood did not survive the fire.

Owns Suamox

list.name: Salt and Emerald Monopoly
list.text: The Muisca sat on the only major salt deposits in the northern Andes, mined open-pit at Zipaquira and boiled from concentrated brine at Nemocon and Tausa. They also controlled the emerald veins at Muzo, Somondoco, and Chivor: the only commercial source of fine emeralds anywhere in the pre-Columbian world. State-assigned miners worked the salt pits in seasonal rotation; emerald extraction was reserved to crown-licensed clans who paid tribute in raw stones to the Zipa. Salt loaves and tumbaga gold-copper ingots were the unit of long-distance Muisca trade, exchanged with Caribbean lowlanders for cotton, dried fish, jaguar pelts, and macaw feathers.

list.name: Guecha Warrior Caste
list.text: The Guechas were the Muisca semi-professional warrior class, recruited from the strongest young men of the zybyn-clans, tattooed once on the lip for each enemy killed, and rewarded by the Zipa with land grants, secondary wives, and the license to wear the gold nose-ornament otherwise reserved to caciques. Their core role was frontier defence against the Panche of the Magdalena valley and the Muzo of the western slopes, and dynastic enforcement whenever a cacique-elect refused the prescribed fast at Iraca. The Guechas screamed in chorus on the march to terrify the enemy and fought with throwing-spears, slings, and macana clubs of palmwood, but against Spanish horse and steel they were annihilated at Funza in 1538.
